title: The soldier and the owl, a mast in front, and the seven pairs

slides.heading: Two letters, the last room of the house, and a map
body: Two consonants: one constant, one the rarest here.
A vowel that breaks the reading order.
And a map of half the letters you have not met.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud, every time.

slides.heading: The soldier on the bridge
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **soldier**.
Low class, at the harbour. No new tone rules.

slides.heading: What he does all night
body: A bridge over the creek where the harbour finishes, and a soldier on it all night.
Head curls in, back climbs straight, arch marches down.
The shape is a man pacing a bridge.

slides.heading: The soldier's letter
body: The head curls inward at the start.
A straight climb, then an arch back down.

slides.heading: Write it
body: **Start at the head**, curling inward.
Straight up, then the arch over and down.
Put it at a syllable's **end** and the breath disappears. A plain t-stop.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Soldier, long vowel, snake closing it.
**Out loud before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **ทาง** — a way, a road, a direction.

slides.heading: The owl, and the rarest letter here
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means an **owl**.
The rarest letter in this course: about one character in ten thousand.

slides.heading: So why are we bothering
body: It is rare, and it completes a pattern that is not.
Its partner is the fourth commonest syllable initial in Thai.
A rare letter propping up a common pattern earns its place.

slides.heading: The owl's letter
body: One round eye, with a zigzag crest over the top.
Ear tufts, blinking at a dark harbour.

slides.heading: And its one word
body: **ฮา** — to laugh, the whole-room kind.
The one common word beginning with this letter.
Read it once. The letter earns its place elsewhere.

slides.heading: The last room of the house
body: Back yard, roof, cellar. All three already open.
Today: the **front steps**.
And the one who lives there behaves differently from everybody else.

slides.heading: The one who holds the door
body: His mark goes down **before** the consonant does.
So your eye reaches him first, every time.
And he does not speak until the consonant has gone in.

slides.heading: This is the thing to get right today
body: **Written first. Spoken second.**
You see the vowel before the consonant and say it after.
Six lessons of reading in written order stop here.

slides.heading: Write it, and say it in the right order
body: One upright with a small curve at the top.
Write it **ahead of** the consonant.
Say it aloud until the order stops feeling wrong.

slides.heading: And the short one, which you can already guess
body: **เ-ะ** — the mast in front, and the two hooks **ะ** behind.
The same shortener from lesson four, doing the same job.
Written in full only when nothing follows.

slides.heading: Unless something follows it
body: Two hooks behind, and a final consonant wants that spot.
So they climb and become a small roof over the letter.
**Same sound. Same length.** Only the seat changed. Again.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Mast, giant's letter, the small roof, mouse closing it.
**Watch the order.** Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **เย็น** — cool, and also *evening*.

slides.prompt: You want to write the short e sound twice — once in a syllable ending in k, once in a syllable ending in nothing. What changes between them?

answers: With a final consonant: the hooks become the **roof**.
With nothing following: the hooks stay written out behind.
The sound is identical. Only the spelling reacts.

slides.heading: Now the map
body: Hummers and stoppers tell you their class. You can hear it.
The ones that **breathe or hiss** give you nothing.
So Thai gives each of those sounds **two letters**, in two districts.

slides.heading: Seven sounds, two letters each
body: ค is harbour and ข is temple. Both say kh.
ช is harbour and ฉ is temple. Both say ch.
ท is harbour and ถ is temple. Both say th.
พ is harbour and ผ is temple. Both say ph, and the two are the same figure with the head turned the other way.
ฟ is harbour and ฝ is temple. Both say f, and they differ by the same head turn.
ซ is harbour and ส is temple. Both say s.
ฮ is harbour and ห is temple. Both say h.

slides.prompt: The two letters in a row sound identical. Say what the second one is for, and what you would lose if Thai had only one of them.

answers: One is low class, the other high. Class is half of every tone decision.
One letter per sound would mean only the tones low class can reach.
The second letter is how Thai spells the other tones.

slides.heading: Halfway, and the shape of the rest
body: Fifteen letters, eleven vowels, every room open.
Most of what is left is the temple half of seven pairs you now know.
Next: two letters that both land as n.
